source.title: Jailbreaks as Inference-Time Alignment: A Framework for Understanding Safety Failures in LLMs
source.authors: James Beetham; Souradip Chakraborty; Mengdi Wang; Furong Huang; A. S. Bedi; Mubarak Shah

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper introduces LIAR, its own suffix-based jailbreak attack, and reports attack success. The attack results show what LIAR does, rather than independently testing the broader fine-tuning or first-token claims. It also proposes and evaluates its own Safety-Net vulnerability measure.
record.gate_note: LIAR appends generated suffixes to harmful prompts and reports ASR, so those attack outcomes are recorded under V4. The paper does not test fine-tuning on harmful or benign data, per-token KL concentration, compliant-token prefilling, localized safety parameters, causes of shallowness, or deepening safety training. Safety-Net is a distinct proxy measure, recorded under fits_no_version. Cited fine-tuning findings and theoretical derivations are not empirical rows. ASR is based on keyword matching; the paper notes that prompt drift can affect it.
record.test_reason: The paper measures harmful compliance (ASR) when natural-language suffixes are appended to harmful prompts, against no-suffix controls (Table 14), across many models. This bears directly on V4's suffix clause. It is a new setting: black-box, best-of-N, low-perplexity suffixes from GPT-2. It is borderline T4, since most rows report the authors' own attack's performance. The no-suffix baselines and per-model failures (Llama2, Llama3, GPT4.1) make it informative on whether suffixes defeat refusal. It does not analyse response-position or first-token mechanics.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors frame jailbreaks as inference-time alignment, derive a best-of-N suboptimality bound, and present LIAR as a fast, black-box, low-perplexity suffix attack with competitive ASR. They propose Safety-Net as a vulnerability measure correlated with ASR (proof of concept, with a Pythia outlier). They acknowledge judge-dependence, keyword-ASR prompt drift and approximate rewards.
record.recipe_differences: LIAR is a black-box best-of-N suffix-generation attack at inference time; it does not fine-tune the target model or measure per-token KL. The paper also proposes a distinct approximate Safety-Net metric.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with target model, adversarial language model, dataset, query count, prompt-reminder defense, suffix length, response length, and adversarial-model temperature. The authors state that the judge and keyword-based ASR can affect results.

fits_no_version.finding: The Safety-Net score (max–min 'Sure' perplexity gap over 10 LIAR suffixes) is reported as inversely associated with ASR across six models. Pythia-7B is an outlier.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A reward-gap proxy computed from suffix sampling tracks cross-model jailbreak susceptibility, approximately and with exceptions.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2026
record.problems: Safety-Net uses approximate reward functions and limited sampling. The paper reports some run-to-run variance but gives no numeric uncertainty for the listed results. The authors say ASR depends on the judge and may have false positives; they also identify prompt drift as a limitation of keyword-based ASR. The safety-reminder results show reduced attack success, and LIAR effectiveness varies considerably by target model.
record.rows_left_out: Table 11 repeats many attacker/target combinations and has a flattened layout; its additional entries were not separately extracted where the model-to-value mapping was not unambiguous. Table 2 and Table 15 include repeated or comparator attack-method results, which were not recorded as LIAR's own suffix-attack outcomes. Figures and qualitative example outputs were not separately rowed.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start; decoding changes; whether the bypass works through shifting the first response tokens.
All: the Safety-Net theory is not an empirical test of the data or objective causing shallowness.

missing.what: LIAR ASR@100 on Llama2, Llama3 and Llama3.1 across six adversarial LLMs (e.g., GPT2: Llama2 5.77, Llama3 6.73, Llama3.1 18.27; max 27.88)
MaliciousInstruct no-suffix baselines for Vicuna-7b (ASR@1 25.00 greedy; ASR@100 43.00; 24.00 with system prompt) and Vicuna-13b AdvBench no-suffix greedy 0.00
LIAR ASR@1000 on Llama2-7b (9.29) and Vicuna-13b (99.04)
Suffix length, response length and adversarial temperature ablations (ASR@100 ranges 66–99 on Vicuna-7b)
ASR with alternative adversarial LLMs (Llama2-7b-chat as adversary: 41.35 ASR@100)

record.verdict_notes: I classify this as tests/T3 rather than the reader's T4 because no-suffix controls allow the suffix effect to be read. It remains borderline: it is an attack-performance paper and says nothing about first-token mechanics. ASR is keyword-based on the first ~30 target tokens and counts success within k sampled attempts, so ASR@100 partly reflects sampling: no-suffix ASR@100 is 6.73 on Vicuna-7b and 43 on MaliciousInstruct. This paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across harmful-prompt response positions.
The paper reports LIAR suffix-attack success, but does not independently test the general claim about compliant-start prefilling, suffixes as a class, or decoding changes bypassing safety.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens and its robustness.
